content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.
When this app is finished, what should be different for you compared with how you manage bookmarks today?

Honestly, right now my bookmarks are a mess — they're just a long flat list in my browser and I can never find anything. So the big thing is that when this is done, I'd want saving a link to actually be useful. When I paste a link in, I'd love it to just grab the page's title and a little description on its own, so I'm not typing all that out myself.

And then I want to actually *find* things later — search that looks at what I saved, and a way to organize with labels or tags so I can pull up, say, all my recipes or all my work articles in one click.

A few other things that'd make my life better: being able to mark something as "read this later" and see just those, jot a note to myself on a link, and clean up old stuff without losing it forever — like tucking it away rather than deleting it outright.

That's the gist of where my head is. Where would you like to start?

content: For duplicate detection, should addresses that lead to the same page still count as one bookmark when the pasted version only adds an ending slash, jumps to a section on the page, or includes advertising-tracking information?

Honestly, yes — to me those all feel like "the same page," so I'd expect it to treat them as one bookmark rather than nagging me to make a fresh copy.

Thinking through your three cases the way I'd actually run into them:

- The extra slash at the end — that's the same page, no question. Should count as already saved.
- Jumping to a section partway down the page — it's still the same article, I've just landed lower on it. I'd want that recognized as the one I already have.
- The advertising or tracking gibberish tacked on the end — that stuff isn't really part of the address to me; it's just junk that got stuck on when I copied it. Two links that are identical except for that should absolutely be seen as the same page.

So across all three, I'd want it to spot that I've already got the page and take me to that existing bookmark, same as the plain duplicate did earlier. The one caution I'd add from my side: don't get so aggressive about it that two *genuinely different* pages on the same site get mistaken for one — if the real part of the address is different, those are different bookmarks. But for the trivial trailing-slash, jump-to-section, and tracking-junk cases you listed, treat them as one.

The real application is ready at [http://maker:4000](http://maker:4000).

Verification passed against all 17 approved scenarios, including saving fetched and edited details, duplicate handling, search, tags, ordering, read-later, notes, archive/delete safeguards, original-page links, empty/error states, and batch actions. All 11 internal tests and the full integrated browser workflow passed.

The library starts empty so you can experience the real first-use flow. Please try the application and tell me whether you accept it as the completed software for this cycle.

I've had a proper go at the real app, not just taken your word for it — and it genuinely does the things we agreed on.

I tried it from a truly empty library, and the first-use invitation greeted me just as before. Saving worked: I put in a link, and it kept my edited title, description, my formatted note, and my tags exactly as I entered them. A nonsense address got stopped with a clear "enter a complete web address" message, and a page that wouldn't respond let me fill in the details and save it manually rather than losing the link.

The duplicate handling really impressed me — I re-entered the same page with a slash on the end, and again with a jumble of tracking bits and a jump-to-section on it, and both times it recognized I already had that page rather than making a copy; a genuinely different page on the same site was correctly treated as new, which is the caution I asked for. Search found things by title, note, and address regardless of capitalization; tags suggested themselves and refused to create near-duplicates; read-later, ordering, and opening the original page all behaved. Bulk tagging added a tag to a group without wiping the tags they already had, batch archiving and read-later worked, and — reassuringly — the app flat-out refused to permanently delete anything that wasn't archived first, exactly the safety net we built. (I tidied my test entries afterward, so your library's empty again for a real first run.)

This is the app I set out to have. I accept it as complete for this cycle.

One small note for a *future* round, nothing that holds this up: down the line I might like a couple of extra conveniences like saving a favorite search as a reusable view, and bringing bookmarks in from or out to my browser. Please just jot those down for later — they're not part of what we agreed this time, and I'm happy with what you've delivered.
